subject: Automotive & EVs
title: Model 3 Goes Mass Market
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Model 3 Goes Mass Market.

hook.text: When Tesla opened Model 3 reservations in 2016, 400,000 people paid $1,000 each in one week.

buildup.text: The $35,000 base price promised a Tesla for regular buyers, not just the wealthy.

discovery.text: Production was brutal. Musk slept in the factory as build quality and delays plagued early output.

twist.text: Skeptics predicted failure. Instead, Model 3 became the best-selling EV in history by 2020.

climax.text: It forced every major automaker to accelerate their own EV plans or risk losing market share.

punchline.text: Model 3 made EVs a mainstream choice, not a niche.

quiz.question: How many Model 3 reservations came in the first week?

details.summary: The Tesla Model 3, launched in 2017 at a starting price of $35,000, was the first affordable long-range electric car aimed at the mass market, becoming the best-selling EV in history within a few years.
details.whyItMatters: The Model 3 proved that mainstream consumers would buy electric cars if range and price were competitive. Its success forced every major automaker to take EVs seriously.
takeaways: It launched with a $35,000 base price and over 300 miles of range
Over 400,000 people placed deposits before production began
It became the world's best-selling electric car by 2020

faq.question: Was the $35,000 Model 3 actually available at that price?
faq.answer: Briefly. Tesla struggled to produce the base model profitably and eventually removed it from the website, pushing buyers toward more expensive versions. The entry price has since risen above $40,000.

faq.question: Why was the Model 3 so difficult to manufacture?
faq.answer: Tesla's ambitious automation targets failed, leading to production hell with quality issues and delays. Elon Musk admitted that excessive automation was a mistake and the company had to add more human workers.
